transcript.text: w/m finally died after 12 yrs, whats the best one to buy under £400? family of 5

For a family of 5 the most important factor is drum size: go for 9kg minimum, ideally 10kg. That means fewer loads and room for duvets. Here are solid options under £400 (prices fluctuate, so check AO, Currys, Argos, and John Lewis for current deals):

## Top picks

Best overall: Bosch Series 4 (9kg, e.g. WGG04409GB / WAN28259GB range)
• Very reliable, quiet, and good at stain removal
• Often £380–£450, so watch for sales; it regularly dips under £400
• The closest thing to "buy it and forget it for another 12 years"

Best value big drum: Hisense 10kg (WFGE/WF3S series)
• Usually £300–£350 for 10kg, which is hard to beat
• Steam function, decent energy rating
• Less proven long-term than Bosch, but well reviewed

Good all-rounder: Beko 9–10kg (e.g. B5W5941AW / B3W51041IW)
• £300–£380
• Often comes with a longer warranty when registered
• Cheap parts and easy repairs

Feature-packed: Samsung 9kg EcoBubble or Haier 9–10kg
• Good quick washes and quiet inverter motors
• Haier often includes a 5-year warranty; Samsung gives long cover on the motor

## Checklist for a busy family
• 9–10kg drum
• 1400rpm spin: clothes dry faster, which matters with lots of laundry
• Energy rating A or B: with daily washing, the running costs add up
• Good quick wash (30–40 min for a full load, not just a tiny 15-min half load)
• Inverter/brushless motor: quieter and usually longer-lasting
• Warranty: favour 5-year cover where offered

## Practical tips
• Measure your space. Most machines are 60cm wide, but 10kg models can be deeper (~60–65cm).
• Add delivery, installation, and old machine removal. This is often £20–£40 extra. AO and Currys do it all in one visit, sometimes next day.
• Read Which? reviews if you have access, as they test reliability over time.

If I had to pick one: a Bosch Series 4 9kg if you can catch it under £400, otherwise a Hisense or Beko 10kg for maximum capacity per pound.

Do you want me to help narrow it down by anything else, like noise (open-plan kitchen?) or integrated vs freestanding?
thanks. tbh would fix the old one if its cheap. it stopped mid-cycle 2 days ago with water still in, wont drain, just hums. any idea whats wrong?

Good news: humming, stopped mid-cycle, and water left in the drum is the classic sign of a blocked drain pump. The hum is the pump motor trying to turn but being jammed. It's often a free fix, and the worst case is usually a £15–£40 part.

## Try this first (free, ~30 mins)

1. Unplug the machine and turn off the taps behind it.

2. Get ready for water. There could be 10–20 litres in there. Lay down old towels and grab a baking tray or shallow container (a bucket won't fit under).

3. Find the drain filter. It's usually behind a small flap at the bottom front corner. Many machines have a thin emergency drain hose next to it. Pull that out, unplug the cap, and drain into your tray bit by bit.

4. Unscrew the filter slowly (anticlockwise) once most of the water's out. Expect coins, hair grips, buttons, kids' toy bits, socks, or a gunky mess. With 3 kids, it's very likely something's in there.

5. Check the pump impeller. Look into the hole where the filter was. You'll see a small plastic paddle. Poke it with a finger. It should spin freely, maybe with a slightly lumpy feel (that's normal, it's magnetic). If it's jammed or something's wrapped round it, clear it.

6. Refit the filter firmly, plug in, and run a rinse/spin or drain cycle.

## If it still hums and won't drain

• Check the drain hose at the back for kinks, and where it connects under the sink. The sink trap or spigot can block up, especially with a new sink or dishwasher installed.
• Pump is seized or dead. If the impeller won't turn at all, or spins but the pump doesn't work, the pump needs replacing. They're usually £15–£40 online (search your model number plus "drain pump"). It's a fairly easy DIY job on most machines, with YouTube videos for most models.
• Blockage in the sump hose between the drum and pump (usually a sock). It's a bit more work to get to.

## Is it worth a repair person?

A callout plus pump replacement is typically £80–£150. For a 12-year-old machine that's otherwise been fine, that's worth it compared to £350+ for a new one, especially if you try the filter yourself first.

One heads-up: the door will stay locked until the water's out. Don't force it, as it'll unlock a couple of minutes after draining.

What make and model is it? I can tell you exactly where the filter is and which pump it takes.
its a Hotpoint, WMBF944P on the door rim. never knew there was a filter tbh. water's still in the drum so i'll unplug it first, where is it?

Unplugging first is exactly right. With water in the drum, the door may stay locked until it's drained, so don't force it.

## Where the filter is on your Hotpoint

On the WMBF944P it's at the bottom front, behind the plinth (kickstrip) panel below the door. Depending on the exact version you'll see either:
• A small flap in the bottom corner (usually right). Press or pry it open with a fingernail or coin.
• A full-width strip along the bottom. Pop it off by pushing a flat-head screwdriver into the slots or gap at the top edge and levering gently. It clips off.

Behind it you'll see a round cap about 6–8cm across with a grip handle. That's the filter.

## Draining it (this is the messy bit)

Many Hotpoints of this age don't have an emergency drain hose, so the water comes out through the filter itself. To keep it under control:

1. Towels down around the front, plus a baking tray or roasting tin under the filter.
2. Optional but helpful: tilt the machine back slightly and wedge something (a book, a block of wood) under the front feet. That raises the filter so less water rushes out at once.
3. Unscrew the filter anticlockwise just a quarter turn or so until water starts trickling. Don't take it straight out or you'll get a flood.
4. When the tray's nearly full, screw it back tight, empty the tray, and repeat. With a full drum this can take 10–20 trays, so be patient.
5. Once it's just dribbling, unscrew it fully, pull it out and clear any gunk or objects.
6. Spin the impeller in the hole with your finger and remove anything wrapped around it.
7. Rinse the filter, screw it back in firmly, refit the panel, plug in, and run a rinse and spin.

If it drains and spins normally after that, you've just saved yourself £350. If it still hums with water in, let me know what you found in the filter and whether the impeller spins, and we can work out the next step.
ok will give it a go, just got towels and a tray. will report back what i find

Good luck! A few last tips before you start:

• Go slow on the first turn. The water comes out faster than you'd expect, so loosen just enough for a steady trickle.
• Have a second tray or bowl ready so you can swap while emptying the first, rather than screwing the filter back in every time.
• The water may smell bad after sitting for 2 days. That's normal and nothing to worry about.
• Keep any clothes inside until it's drained. Once the water's out, the door lock usually releases after a minute or two.
• Run a hot empty wash (60°C or higher) afterwards with a bit of washing machine cleaner or a cup of white vinegar to freshen it up.

Report back with what you find in the filter and whether the impeller spins freely. Fingers crossed it's just a rogue sock or a few coins! 🤞
